passage: Come, sit, Meera beta. You asked how to help a friend without disappearing yourself, so listen to Pooja's story. I was twenty. My friend Vasudha called me at two, at four, in the middle of lectures. I felt so important, beta, the only one she trusted. And so tired that I fell asleep on the bus. My mother said, "You are not her doctor." I was angry with Ma for a week. Then one night I said, "Vasudha, I love you, but I can't be your only support. Let's meet the college counsellor together, and call your sister too." She cried. I cried. I sat with her at the first appointment, but I stopped picking up every single call. It felt like betrayal then. It was also the first time she got real help.

qa.q: How old was Pooja when Vasudha started calling at all hours?
How did Pooja feel about being Vasudha's only support?
qa.a: Important and needed, yet so tired that Pooja fell asleep on the bus.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that joined care with limits?
qa.a: Pooja suggested going to the college counsellor together, urged Vasudha to call her sister, and stopped picking up every single call.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when Pooja stopped answering every call?
qa.a: She may have feared being dropped, and she cried, but the change also led her to real help at the appointment.

grounding: An elder recalls a friend who relied on her for everything: needed and drained, she set limits and steered the friend toward professional help.

passage:
In the Singapore student flat, Mina's phone buzzed at 2 am. Xin again. "Can't sleep. Can you talk?" Last night it was 1 am; the night before, 3. Xin called about everything: a cold email from a lecturer, a strange noise in the corridor, what to eat for lunch.

Mina loved being needed. She also had a stats exam at nine and hadn't slept properly in a week.

She answered. "I'm here for ten minutes, Xin. Then I need to sleep." Xin went quiet, hurt.

The next afternoon, over noodles, Mina tried again. "I care about you. But I can't be the only one you lean on. Would you try the student counselling service? I'll walk you there."

Xin frowned, then nodded slowly. "Maybe also the Thursday choir. My cousin sings there."

That night Mina's phone was silent until morning.

qa.q: At what time did Mina's phone buzz?
What was Mina feeling about Xin's constant calls?
qa.a: Mina felt both needed and drained, loving to help but exhausted before an exam.

qa.q: What small step helped both of them?
qa.a: Mina set a time limit on the call and then, when calm, suggested the counselling service and offered to walk Xin there.

qa.q: How might Xin have felt when Mina said ten minutes?
qa.a: Xin felt hurt at first, going quiet, perhaps afraid of losing the one person she relied on.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose friend depends on her at all hours, setting limits kindly and encouraging professional and other support.

passage:
The college counselling centre had a waiting room with plastic chairs and a jar of mints. Kashish sat beside Nazia, who was jiggling her foot. For three months Nazia had called Kashish for everything: panic before class, arguments with her parents, whether to reply to a message. Twice at 4 am.

Kashish had skipped her own internship interview last week to sit with her. She felt proud of being trusted and so tired she could barely think.

Yusuf, the peer mentor at the front desk, caught Kashish's eye. Last week he had told her, "You're doing a lot. It's okay to share it."

When Nazia's name was called, she grabbed Kashish's hand. "Come in with me?"

Kashish squeezed back and let go. "I'll be right here after. This part is yours." Nazia went in alone.

qa.q: What was in the waiting room besides plastic chairs?
qa.a: There was a jar of mints.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel about being Nazia's main support?
qa.a: Kashish felt proud of being trusted but also deeply tired, having even skipped her own interview.

qa.q: Why was letting Nazia go in alone a caring choice?
qa.a: It kept Kashish's limit while supporting Nazia in building her own relationship with a professional.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see what Kashish was carrying?
qa.a: Yusuf seems to see her as overloaded and wants her to know sharing the load with others is okay.

grounding: The counselling-centre scene shows a young woman leaned on by a friend for everything, keeping limits and encouraging professional support.
